chief_complaint: nasal polyps, chronic asthma, and acute wheezing attack after taking aspirin or ibuprofen
hpi_details: 48M with chronic rhinosinusitis and nasal polyps presenting with acute severe bronchospasm and facial flushing within 60 minutes of taking ibuprofen for headache.
ideas: He thinks the headache pills he swallowed were expired or went down the wrong pipe and irritated his lungs into a massive asthma attack.
concerns: He is worried that he could suddenly suffocate if he has another violent attack while working alone at his desk.
expectations: He hopes to get immediate medication to open his airways and clear guidance on which pain relievers are safe for his headaches.
pmh: Asthma; chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps

clinical_knowledge.topic: Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease (AERD / Samter's Triad) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease (AERD / Samter's Triad) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management is strict avoidance of aspirin and other COX-1-inhibiting NSAIDs, with aspirin desensitization under specialist supervision as a long-term option, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: nasal polyps, chronic asthma, and acute wheezing attack after taking aspirin or ibuprofen
Key HPI features: 48M with chronic rhinosinusitis and nasal polyps presenting with acute severe bronchospasm and facial flushing within 60 minutes of taking ibuprofen for headache.
Objective/Exam findings: Diffuse expiratory wheeze and facial flushing during the acute reaction; nasal exam shows polyposis; no urticaria.
Relevant background/PMH: Asthma; chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease (AERD / Samter's Triad).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to True IgE-mediated NSAID allergy (urticaria/anaphylaxis type) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe bronchospasm requiring emergency treatment after NSAID use.
management_principles: Strictly avoid aspirin and other COX-1-inhibiting NSAIDs; consider aspirin desensitization under specialist supervision for long-term control
Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease AERD Samter Triad: nasal polyps, chronic asthma, and acute wheezing attack after taking aspirin or ibuprofen. 48M with chronic rhinosinusitis and nasal polyps presenting with acute severe bronchospasm and facial flushing within 60 minutes of taking ibuprofen for headache.
reference_soap.objective: Diffuse expiratory wheeze and facial flushing during the acute reaction; nasal exam shows polyposis; no urticaria.
reference_soap.assessment: Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease (AERD / Samter's Triad) with acute NSAID-induced bronchospasm.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Treat the acute bronchospasm with standard asthma exacerbation therapy (bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroids as needed); do not give aspirin or any NSAID acutely. 2. Strictly avoid aspirin and other COX-1-inhibiting NSAIDs going forward (acetaminophen and COX-2-selective agents are generally better tolerated). 3. Refer to allergy/immunology for consideration of supervised aspirin desensitization and to ENT for polyp management.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease AERD Samter Triad

Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for allergy_immunology
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: The triad of asthma, nasal polyps, and acute bronchospasm within an hour of taking aspirin or any NSAID — a pseudoallergic COX-1 reaction, not true IgE allergy.
differentials: Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps alone
red_flags: Severe bronchospasm requiring emergency treatment after NSAID use
Facial flushing with breathing difficulty — can mimic anaphylaxis

must_ask.say: How soon after taking the ibuprofen did your breathing get worse?

must_ask.objective: The triad — nasal polyps and asthma history
must_ask.say: Do you have nasal polyps or chronic sinus problems along with your asthma?
Have you lost your sense of smell?
Has this happened with other pain relievers like aspirin before?
Did your face flush or feel hot during the reaction?

history.answer: I took an ibuprofen for a headache about forty minutes ago, and shortly after, my chest tightened up and I started wheezing heavily.
It began suddenly about thirty to forty minutes after I swallowed the ibuprofen tablet, and it has gotten progressively worse.
Right now I feel short of breath even sitting still, and it is uncomfortable to speak in full sentences.
The shortness of breath has been steady and worsening since it started, not coming and going in waves.
I don't have trouble lying flat or wake up gasping at night; this came on purely after taking the painkiller.
Taking that ibuprofen was the immediate trigger; normally cold dry air can make me wheeze a bit, but never this badly.
Yes, I can clearly hear a high-pitched whistling and wheezing sound every time I exhale.
I have a dry, tight cough from my chest feeling constricted, but no phlegm and no fever at all.
My chest feels uncomfortably tight and squeezed, but there is no sharp stabbing or heavy crushing pain.
My heart feels like it's racing because I am struggling to breathe, but I haven't felt faint or dizzy.
No, I haven't coughed up any blood.
No, my legs and ankles are not swollen, and my weight has been completely steady.
No leg soreness or swelling, and I haven't had recent surgery, cast immobilization, or long plane travel.
No unusual fatigue, skin paleness, or dark tarry stools.
I feel anxious because I can't catch my breath, but my fingers and lips are not tingling or numb.
I was diagnosed with asthma about five years ago, but it has generally been mild and well controlled.
I have a rescue albuterol inhaler at home, but I rarely need it and unfortunately didn't have it on me today.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used electronic cigarettes in my life.
I work an office desk job, so I am not exposed to industrial dust, asbestos, birds, or chemical fumes.
I took a single four hundred milligram ibuprofen pill for a tension headache about forty minutes before this started.
The shortness of breath, wheezing, and facial warmth started within forty-five minutes of swallowing the pill.
Yes, I have suffered from chronic sinus congestion and was diagnosed with nasal polyps about three years ago.
Yes, I actually lost almost my entire sense of smell a couple of years ago due to the chronic sinus polyps.
Yes, my face and neck became intensely flushed, hot, and red right as the breathing difficulty began.
A few months ago I took an aspirin for back pain and had mild chest tightness and a stuffy nose, but nothing as severe as this.
No, I don't have any raised itchy hives, welts, or swelling of my lips and tongue.
I thought maybe the ibuprofen I took for my headache was bad or went down the wrong way and set off my asthma.
I'm terrified that my throat will completely close up and I'll suffocate when no one is around to help me at work.
I want something fast to help me breathe normally again, and I need to know what painkillers I can safely take for my headaches.
Aside from my asthma and chronic nasal polyposis, I have no history of high blood pressure, heart disease, or diabetes.
I had endoscopic sinus surgery to remove polyps two years ago, but they unfortunately recurred.
I do not take any daily prescription medications or regular supplements.
I was never formally tested for drug allergies, but both aspirin and ibuprofen have now triggered wheezing attacks.
I drink one or two glasses of wine socially on weekends, though wine sometimes makes my nose stuffy.
I work full-time in administrative consulting and live with my wife in an apartment.
My mother had allergic rhinitis, but there is no family history of severe asthma or medication allergies.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, pulse 100 beats/min, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, temperature 36.7 C, oxygen saturation 94% on room air.
Patient appears in moderate respiratory distress with noticeable facial flushing, speaking in broken phrases, with no cyanosis or finger clubbing.
Marked erythematous facial flushing over cheeks and forehead; no hives, welts, or angioedema.
Bilateral pale, glistening, grayish mucosal polyps visible in nasal passages; oropharynx clear without uvular deviation or swelling.
Mild tenderness on palpation over bilateral maxillary sinuses.
Symmetric chest expansion with mild intercostal and suprasternal retractions; no chest wall tenderness.
Resonant to percussion bilaterally across all lung fields.
Diffuse expiratory wheezing throughout all lung fields bilaterally with a prolonged expiratory phase and no crackles.
Tachycardic regular rhythm with normal S1 and S2, without murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
No pitting edema in bilateral lower extremities.
Calves are supple, symmetric, and non-tender without swelling or erythema.
